nameStory: The Florida hammock sandmat gets its name from its preferred habitat in Florida's hammocks - those slightly elevated, wooded islands that rise above the surrounding wetlands like natural hammocks. The "sandmat" part describes its low, creeping growth habit that forms dense mats along sandy soils, carpeting the ground like a living blanket.
description: Florida hammock sandmat is a tiny, sprawling annual plant that hugs the ground in low, spreading mats. This delicate member of the spurge family rarely grows more than a few inches tall, instead sending out slender stems that creep along sandy surfaces. Like all spurges, it produces a milky white sap when broken and has small, inconspicuous flowers that lack true petals. In New England, this southern visitor is extremely rare, with only one recorded observation.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms very low, creeping mats that sprawl along the ground, with thin stems that feel delicate to the touch and rarely rise above 2-3 inches high

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, oval leaves arranged opposite each other along the stems, often less than a quarter-inch long and smooth to the touch with a slightly waxy feel

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Extremely small, greenish-white flowers tucked in leaf joints that lack showy petals - you'll need to look closely as they're easily missed

idTips.label: Sap
idTips.description: Breaks stems to reveal the characteristic milky white latex sap of all spurges - this sap can be irritating to skin so avoid touching your eyes

habitat: In its native range, Florida hammock sandmat thrives in sandy soils of coastal areas and woodland edges. The single New England observation suggests it may occasionally appear as a rare waif or accidental introduction, possibly in disturbed sandy areas like parking lots, construction sites, or near ports where seeds might arrive with transported materials.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in warm weather, forming small rosettes of tiny leaves that begin spreading outward in thin mats.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and produce their inconspicuous flowers, with the mat-forming growth habit most evident during peak growing season.
seasonality.fall: Flowers develop into small seed capsules that split to disperse seeds, while the annual plants begin to decline as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: As an annual plant adapted to warm climates, it dies back completely with frost, leaving only seeds to potentially germinate the following year.

funFact: This tiny plant is so rare in New England that finding one would be like discovering botanical treasure - with only a single recorded observation, you'd be more likely to spot a celebrity walking down the street than to encounter this diminutive southern wanderer in a New England landscape!
confusionNotes: Could potentially be confused with other small, mat-forming spurges like spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat, but its extremely small size and the rarity of finding it this far north are key distinguishing features. The milky sap when broken confirms it as a spurge rather than other small, creeping plants.
contextualKnowledge: Like many spurges, the milky sap contains compounds that can cause skin and eye irritation, so it's best observed rather than handled. The extreme rarity in New England means any suspected sighting should be photographed and reported to local botanists, as it would represent a significant range extension or unusual occurrence.
compareHints: Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit. While spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat also creep along the ground, they're generally larger and more robust, and seaside sandmat, though similar in habitat preferences, has more linear leaves and is typically found right along the coast rather than inland sandy areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
